teaser: A song at the piano, a hand around her waist, and the second she decides to leave.
review_notes:
The handwritten notes in the top corners of this photograph are Hunt's own technical notes on varnishing and retouching (dates 1864 and 86 legible); normally covered by the arched frame. Please confirm reading.
Fairbairn asking Hunt to repaint the face: standard account; date of repainting around 1856.
Room rented at Woodbine Villa, St John's Wood: check.
Frame motifs (marigolds for sorrow, bells for warning) and the verse from Proverbs: check wording.
Floor music: Edward Lear's setting of Tennyson's 'Tears, Idle Tears'.
The cat's prey (a bird) is small in this image; spot is sized to cover cat and the area just below.
Annie Miller's biography (barmaid, engagement to Hunt): check wording.

lesson.text: What does a change of mind look like? Not the reasons for it, not what comes after. The exact second. William Holman Hunt set himself that problem in 1853, and he chose the hardest possible case: a woman in the middle of a song, in a man's lap, in a house he pays for.

Victorian viewers understood the situation at once. She is a kept mistress, set up by a wealthy lover in a rented villa. He has been playing the piano and singing, one arm still around her. Something in the song has reached her. She is halfway to her feet.

lesson.title: Two faces, two hands
lesson.text: He has not noticed anything yet. She has stopped hearing him.

spots.title: Her face
spots.text: Eyes wide and fixed on something outside the picture, lips parted. She is looking toward the light, toward where you stand.

spots.title: His face
spots.text: Head thrown back, mouth open, still singing and smiling up at her. He thinks this is the same afternoon it was a minute ago.

spots.title: Her hands
spots.text: Clasped tight. There are rings on her fingers, but the finger where a wedding ring would go is bare. In 1853 that told the whole story.

spots.title: His hand
spots.text: His open hand still lies across her lap, palm up, cuff bright against the dark sleeve. It holds nothing now. She has already risen out of it.

lesson.text: Her face is the center of the picture, and it is not the face Hunt first painted. The man who bought the work, the industrialist Thomas Fairbairn, found her original expression of anguish too painful to live with and asked Hunt to change it. Hunt repainted it. What you see is the softer second version.
Hunt rented a room in a real villa of this kind in St John's Wood, a London suburb known for such arrangements, so that every piece of furniture would be the right sort of wrong.

Hunt was a founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, a group of young British painters who, from 1848, rejected soft, flattering studio painting. They wanted bright color, hard focus and truth in every inch, the way early Italian painters worked before Raphael. In this room nothing is blurred, and nothing is innocent.
What is she staring at? Hunt answers behind her back. The wall there, with its gilded frame and its open window, is not a wall at all. It is glass, and it shows what the room faces.
The back of the room holds a large mirror. Find her reflection in it.

spots.title: Seen from behind
spots.text: The back of her head and her loose hair appear in the mirror, against a reflected window full of sunlit leaves. So the garden is in front of her, on our side. She is looking out at spring.

lesson.text: That is the hinge of the picture. Behind her, a room stuffed with new, shiny, purchased things. In front of her, daylight and a garden. The critic John Ruskin, who defended the painting in a letter to The Times in 1854, wrote of the “fatal newness” of the furniture: nothing here has ever been part of a home.
Pre-Raphaelite pictures are meant to be read. Every object is painted sharply because every object is evidence.
Now the floor and the corners. Hunt has scattered warnings around her like props on a stage. None of them is hidden, and each shows what she will be if she stays.

lesson.title: Warnings on the floor
lesson.text: Three small disasters, all within reach of her skirt.

spots.title: The cat
spots.text: Under the table a cat crouches, eyes shining. It has been toying with a bird, and it too has been interrupted. Predator and prey, mirroring the couple above.

spots.title: The glove
spots.text: A soiled glove, dropped on the carpet. Used, then tossed aside. Viewers read it as her future.

spots.title: Tangled thread
spots.text: Bright strands of yarn spill off her embroidery frame and knot on the floor. A piece of work coming undone.

lesson.text: The cruelest detail is that the lover caused all this himself. He chose the song. Hunt lets you read the title on the music stand, and then gives you a second song lying on the floor.
Ruskin singled out the lace hem of her dress, which Hunt painted thread by thread. Its whiteness, he wrote, would soon be soiled with dust and rain if she ended up on the street.

lesson.title: Two songs
lesson.text: Both are about remembering.

spots.title: On the piano
spots.text: The sheet reads “Oft in the Stilly Night”, a popular song by Thomas Moore about lying awake and recalling the joys of childhood. He sang it for fun. She heard the words.

spots.title: On the floor
spots.text: A rolled score, still partly in its blue wrapper: a setting of Tennyson's poem “Tears, Idle Tears”, about days that are gone. It has not even been opened yet.

lesson.text: The model was Annie Miller, a young barmaid Hunt had met near his studio. He planned to have her educated and to marry her, a rescue of his own. It did not work out. He left for the Holy Land in 1854, she went her own way, and the engagement ended.

Hunt showed the picture at the Royal Academy in 1854 beside another canvas, “The Light of the World”, in which Christ knocks at a closed door at night. He thought of them as a pair: one shows the knock, the other shows someone hearing it.
Hunt designed the frame himself. It carries marigolds, a flower of sorrow, and bells for warning, with a verse from the Book of Proverbs about singing songs to a heavy heart.
That frame has an arched top, and it normally hides the corners of the picture. This photograph shows the painting without it, which is why a few things are visible that museum visitors never see.

spots.title: Hunt's notes
spots.text: Handwriting in the corner the frame usually covers. Hunt recorded how the picture was varnished and treated, with dates decades after 1853. He kept caring for it.

spots.title: The clock
spots.text: A gilt clock under a glass dome. Time is passing, and it is sealed in with everything else in the room.

spots.title: The window
spots.text: The open window and garden exist only as a reflection in the mirror. White light, green leaves: the one natural thing in the picture.

spots.title: The bow
spots.text: A pink ribbon at her throat, and under it a loose white gown. She is not dressed to go out. This is indoor clothing, another sign of how she lives.

spots.title: His hat
spots.text: A top hat set down on the table. He is a visitor here. He will pick it up and go home.

spots.title: The hem
spots.text: White cotton lace, every eyelet accounted for. This is the passage Ruskin praised.

spots.title: The date
spots.text: Hunt's monogram and the year 1853, tucked into the bottom corner of the carpet.

lesson.text: Hunt stops the clock at the second she rises. He does not show whether she reaches the door, or what a woman with no money and no name does on the other side of it. Does she go?

quiz.question: What is the woman's situation?
quiz.explanation: Her bare ring finger and the showy rented room told Victorian viewers she was a mistress.

quiz.question: How do we know what she is looking at?
options: A mirror behind her reflects a window and garden
A label on the frame says so
quiz.explanation: The mirror shows the sunlit garden that lies in front of her.

quiz.question: Why did Hunt repaint her face?
options: The buyer found her original expression too painful
quiz.explanation: Thomas Fairbairn asked for a less anguished expression.

quiz.question: What does the cat under the table echo?
options: The man toying with the woman
quiz.explanation: The cat with its bird mirrors the predator and prey above.

quiz.question: Which critic defended the painting in The Times?
quiz.explanation: Ruskin wrote a letter explaining its details, including the “fatal newness” of the furniture.

quiz.question: Which painting did Hunt exhibit as its companion?
quiz.explanation: He paired it with his picture of Christ knocking at a door.

facts.explanation: She has rings on her fingers, but none on the wedding finger.

facts.text: The song on the piano is about remembering a happier past.
facts.explanation: “Oft in the Stilly Night” recalls the joys of childhood.

facts.text: The garden is visible through a window directly behind her.
facts.explanation: It is a reflection in a mirror, so the real window is in front of her.
